family_history: Mother had memory problems in 80s, etiology unknown

social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband; son visits weekly

patient.chief_complaint: Difficulty walking, urinary leakage, and memory decline over the past two years — family brought in for evaluation
patient.history_present_illness: A 74-year-old left-handed retired pharmacist with hypertension and osteoporosis was admitted for evaluation of a two-year progressive decline in gait, bladder control, and memory. Her husband, a retired engineer, has kept meticulous notes of her functional decline and brought these to the appointment. He documents the onset approximately two years ago when she began walking more slowly and taking smaller steps. She fell once on uneven pavement nine months ago and sustained a wrist contusion; she has used a cane since then. She describes her legs as 'not obeying her' and says she feels unsteady on her feet constantly. Her urinary urgency began approximately 18 months ago with three to four episodes of leakage per week, mainly associated with urgency or delayed response; she wears protective underwear daily. Cognitive symptoms include increasing word-finding difficulty, misplacing objects, difficulty calculating change, and repeating herself in conversation. She is an extremely detail-oriented person by training and is acutely aware of her deficits, which distresses her greatly. She denies headache, diplopia, tremor, or numbness. Her alendronate was not stopped prior to admission as there is no surgical intervention planned at this stage. Head CT obtained by her internist three weeks ago demonstrated hydrocephalus with an Evans index estimated at 0.37 and prompted this admission for NPH evaluation.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place and day. Mildly distressed by her deficits. MoCA 21/30. Impaired delayed recall (2/5), visuospatial mildly impaired (4/5), word fluency reduced (8 words/min). No aphasia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No papilledema. PERRL. Horizontal and vertical gaze intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone and strength. No rigidity. No resting tremor. Mild hip flexor weakness bilaterally (4+/5).
neurological_exam.sensory: Normal to light touch and pinprick throughout. Vibration mildly reduced at ankles.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, magnetic, short-stepped gait with reduced foot clearance. Freezing on initiation. Reduced arm swing. TUG 27 seconds with cane. 10-meter walk 20 seconds. Cannot tandem walk. Pull test — 2 steps backward.
neurological_exam.additional: Bilateral grasp reflexes. No nuchal rigidity. Well-healed right wrist from prior fall.

mri.impression: Florid iNPH features: Evans index 0.39, callosal angle 71°, classic DESH, corpus callosum thinning with upward bowing, transependymal periventricular signal, and hyperdynamic aqueductal flow void. Clinical correlation recommended.

csf.interpretation: Opening pressure: 12 cmH2O. WBC: 1 cell/mcL (N/A PMN/N/A lymph). Protein: 36 mg/dL. Glucose: 70 mg/dL (ratio 0.76). cytology: No malignant cells. beta_amyloid_42: 802 pg/mL (normal). total_tau: 192 pg/mL (normal). phospho_tau: 20 pg/mL (normal).

specialized_test.test_type: High-volume tap trial (40 mL) with TUG and 10-meter walk

findings.freezing: No freezing episodes observed at 24-hour testing

specialized_test.impression: Strongly positive tap trial — 33% TUG improvement and 30% 10-meter walk improvement at 24 hours, with 3-point MoCA improvement. Full triad response confirms iNPH diagnosis and predicts excellent VP shunt outcome.

output.impression: Clearly negative amyloid PET. No concurrent Alzheimer's amyloid pathology. Excellent prognosis for cognitive improvement post-shunting.
Markedly hyperdynamic aqueductal flow (peak velocity 23 cm/s, stroke volume 84 mcL/cycle). Supports iNPH pathophysiology and VP shunt candidacy.

Significant executive function and processing speed improvement post-tap. Frontal-subcortical pattern consistent with iNPH. Memory shows modest improvement. Pattern highly predictive of VP shunt cognitive benefit.

findings.finding: Neurogenic detrusor overactivity — involuntary contractions at 125 mL. Maximum capacity 210 mL. No outlet obstruction, no stress incontinence component.

output.impression: Neurogenic detrusor overactivity consistent with NPH frontal lobe dysfunction. No stress or obstructive component. Expected to improve with VP shunting.

output.test_type: Fall risk assessment and physical therapy evaluation

findings.assessment: Significant gait apraxia, impaired equilibrium responses, history of fall with prior fracture. High-risk for subsequent falls perioperatively.

output.impression: High fall risk. Recommend fall precautions, bilateral hip protector, and supervised ambulation until VP shunt placed and benefit observed. Physical therapy evaluation for assistive device optimization.
recommended_actions: Fall precautions — bed alarm, non-slip footwear
Consider dual-rail walker over cane perioperatively

output.proposed: VP shunt surgery in patient on alendronate
interactions: Alendronate — no relevant drug interactions with neurosurgical anesthesia
warnings: Hold alendronate on day of surgery per anesthesia protocol (aspiration risk with swallowing restrictions)
Resume alendronate once tolerating oral intake post-operatively

differential.key_features: Normal CSF biomarkers (amyloid 802, tau 192), negative amyloid PET (CL 10). Cognitive pattern is frontal not episodic.
Osteoporosis predisposes to fractures but does not explain magnetic gait apraxia. NPH is primary.
Mild periventricular white matter changes; however Evans 0.39 and strongly positive tap trial confirm NPH
Evans 0.39, callosal angle 71°, DESH, positive tap trial — this is pathological, not normal aging

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Evans 0.39, callosal angle 71°, DESH pattern, transependymal signal

optimal_actions.action: High-volume tap trial with quantitative gait analysis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal OP 12 cmH2O; clearly positive (33% TUG)

optimal_actions.action: Amyloid PET to exclude concurrent AD

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Clearly positive tap trial — VP shunt indicated

critical_actions: Confirm low-normal opening pressure at LP (12 cmH2O meets NPH criterion)
Quantify TUG improvement >20% to confirm tap trial positivity
Assess fall risk — high-risk patient with prior osteoporotic fracture
Prompt neurosurgery referral given strongly positive tap trial
contraindicated_actions: Attributing gait decline to osteoporosis or 'normal aging' without NPH workup
Starting bisphosphonate osteoporosis treatment changes without recognizing that NPH gait improvement post-shunt will reduce fall risk independently
Delaying VP shunt referral in a clearly positive tap trial patient
key_reasoning_points: Classic iNPH: Evans 0.39, callosal angle 71°, DESH, 33% TUG improvement post-tap
Low-normal opening pressure (12 cmH2O) — meets required iNPH criterion
Negative amyloid PET and normal CSF biomarkers confirm pure iNPH — no concurrent AD
Osteoporosis is coincidental — does not cause magnetic gait
Fall risk is significant given prior wrist fracture — needs protective measures until shunt placed

red_herrings.data_point: Osteoporosis with prior fall causing wrist fracture
red_herrings.intended_effect: Gait instability and fall attributed to osteoporosis-related fear of falling rather than NPH
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Gait is wide-based and apraxic — primary NPH, not psychomotor fear-of-falling. Tap trial confirms NPH as primary gait disorder.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Concern for familial AD may delay NPH evaluation
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal CSF biomarkers and negative amyloid PET exclude concurrent Alzheimer's disease.

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Straightforward iNPH in a 74-year-old left-handed retired pharmacist — florid MRI findings, strongly positive tap trial, osteoporosis as minor red herring.
